name: Bianca Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half five to check the suckler cows, we've sixty of them, then feed the calves in the old stone shed. Tom and I rent Hollins Farm from the Ashcombe Estate, a hundred and twenty hectares, mostly grass with some spring barley. Most days I'm on the old Massey Ferguson, carting silage or fixing a fence the cows have leaned on. I love calving time, even the cold nights, but the paperwork wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who does the paperwork, and how do you do it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tom does the computer side, grumbling, at the kitchen table on Sunday nights. I keep the herd book on paper, the same blue ledgers my mother used, and I won't change that. Our tenancy comes up for renewal in 2029, and I think about that more than I'd like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the mart: the clever stuff never touches a cow in labour. Farming carries on because somebody still has to be out in the rain. I'd probably add that the money spent on all that hype should have gone to small farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means the same worries as now, which aren't small. The estate could still put the rent up in 2029, and calf prices go up and down like a seesaw. We've about three months of bills put by, and that's it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the cows, keep the barley, and try to put a bit more aside each month before the rent review. Maybe sell twenty store cattle early next autumn instead of keeping them over winter, so the feed bill is lower. I'd go to every tenant farmers' meeting about the 2029 renewals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit relieved, honestly, but not easy. The rent review sits on my chest whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the rent review mean in plain money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the estate adds even fifteen percent, that's our holiday and the new roof on the calf shed gone. Tom says we'd manage, and we would, but only by working harder at fifty-eight than we did at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you talk to about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly Gary next door, who does our contract baling. We stand at the gate and moan about the estate office. My daughter Ruth tells me to read the tenancy on my phone, but I'd rather wait for the paper copy.

say: The clever stuff **never touches** a cow in labour, so farming carries on.
The hype money should have gone to **small farms** instead.
think: My real worry is the **2029 rent review** on our tenancy, not computers.
About **three months** of bills saved feels thin when calf prices swing.
do: Put a set sum aside **each month** before the 2029 rent review.
Sell **twenty store cattle** next autumn to cut the winter feed bill.
Attend every **tenant farmers' meeting** about the estate renewals.
feel: **Relieved** that AI stays small, but the rent review still **weighs** on her.
S0.quote: The estate could still put the rent up in 2029, and calf prices go up and down like a seesaw.
fieldNote: Her pressure is the **tenancy**, not technology: AI Plateau leaves her real worry untouched.
Keeps the herd book in her **mother's ledgers** and lets Tom do the computer work.
Talks about the estate office the way others talk about **the weather**: always there, rarely kind.

steps.text: Keep the sixty suckler cows and the spring barley as they are
Sell twenty store cattle in autumn to cut winter feed
Put money aside every month before the 2029 rent review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to the office people, because they're the ones in for it this time. On a farm it'll be the forms and the ordering that change first. I'd say it at the tenant association too: the estate office will get leaner, not kinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I think it hits Tom's Sunday nights more than my mornings. The subsidy forms, the movement records for the cattle, the feed orders, all that goes onto some app. I won't touch it, so either Tom learns it or we pay someone, and paying someone eats into a thin cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Gary's son Kieran, who's good with computers, to do the cattle records for us for a small fee, maybe fifty a month. I'd keep doing the cows the same way. And I'd push the tenant association to make the estate give us at least a year's notice before any change to the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly. Every few years there's a new thing I'm supposed to learn, and I'm running out of patience for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't touch the apps. What if Tom couldn't do it either?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we'd pay Kieran more and I'd feel stupid about it. I know it's stubborn. But I've only got so many years left on this farm and I want to spend them with the animals, not a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the farm change at all, out in the fields?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, not yet. Robots are slow to come onto rough ground like ours. Maybe the big arable lads down the valley get a robot sprayer, but our cows won't notice.

say: This time it's the **office people** who are in for it, not farmers.
The estate office will get **leaner, not kinder**, and tenants should say so.
think: The **forms and cattle records** move onto apps, which lands on Tom.
Paying someone else to do the screen work eats into a **thin cushion**.
do: Pay Kieran next door about **fifty a month** to keep the cattle records.
Keep the **cows and barley** exactly as they are.
Push the tenant association for **a year's notice** on any rent change.
feel: **Tired** of being told to learn something new every few years.
A little **ashamed** of her stubbornness, but sure of it.
S1.quote: I've only got so many years left on this farm and I want to spend them with the animals, not a screen.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as an **office** problem and her own fields as **untouched**.
Would rather **pay a neighbour** than learn the apps, even though the money is tight.
Turns every change into a question for the **tenant association**: she trusts groups over gadgets.

steps.text: Pay Kieran next door about fifty a month to keep cattle records
Ask the tenant association to demand a year's notice on rent changes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: this is the big companies getting what they want before anyone can stop them. I'd say the government should step in and protect tenant farmers and farm workers, with proper rules. I'd write that to our local paper, because I don't do the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think the estate would look at us in 2029 and see two old tenants on a farm a company could run with robots from 2031. Our renewal lands right in the middle. If they don't renew, Tom and I lose the farm and the house at sixty-one, with three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the tenant association to take the estate to the table now, before 2028, and push for a law that protects sitting tenants. I'd ring our MP's office, which I've never done. I'd stop spending on anything but feed and the vet, and start asking Ruth if we could stay with her for a while if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. I picture packing up the blue ledgers into a cardboard box, and I can't get further than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your job is mostly hands-on. Does it matter that the robots come three years after the thinking AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It matters for the cows, not for the lease. The estate office runs on thinking work, so it changes in 2028 and plans the robots for 2031. They'd only need to stop renewing us in 2029. Two years is nothing when your lease runs out in 2029 and the landlord can see robots coming in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Ruth on the phone that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Ruth not to worry and then cry once I'd hung up. She'd offer us the spare room, and I'd hate needing it.

say: This is **big companies** getting what they want before anyone can stop them.
The government must **protect tenants** and farm workers with proper rules.
think: The estate could **refuse to renew** in 2029 and plan robots for 2031.
Losing the farm means losing the **house** too, at sixty-one, with **three months** saved.
do: Push the tenant association to **negotiate with the estate** before 2028.
Ring the **local MP** and write to the paper for a tenant protection law.
Cut spending to **feed and the vet** only.
feel: **Frightened**, picturing the blue ledgers packed in a cardboard box.
S2.quote: Two years is nothing when your lease runs out in 2029 and the landlord can see robots coming in 2031.
fieldNote: The **timing** is everything: thinking AI changes the estate office before her lease ends.
Hands-on work buys her cows three years but buys her **tenancy nothing**.
Blames **big companies** and turns at once to the association, the MP and the law.
Would lean on her **daughter Ruth** but hates the idea of needing to.

steps.text: Get the tenant association to negotiate with the Ashcombe Estate before 2028
Ring the local MP's office about a sitting-tenant protection law
Cut spending to feed and the vet only
Ask daughter Ruth about staying in her spare room if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: protect the people who work the land, not just the people who own it. I'd say five years is enough time for the government to do something if it wanted to. Whether it wants to is another matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years, our renewal in 2029 comes before the AGI, so we'd likely get another lease. The danger moves to the next one. By then I'd be well into my sixties, and maybe ready to let go anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still go to the association, but I'd also sit down with Tom and work out a date we stop, maybe 2033, while we choose it. I'd save harder, perhaps by selling the oldest ten cows and not replacing them. I'd want to talk to the estate about handing the tenancy to a young couple rather than to a company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sad, but less sick. An ending you can plan is sad, but an ending that's done to you is a different thing altogether.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop earlier than you'd like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, honestly, more than any robot. If the estate offered a fair exit, I might take it at sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want to take over Hollins Farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone young who wants cows, not a company with a screen. I'd fight for that through the association, because it's the one thing I'd still have a say in.

say: Five years is **enough time** for government to act, if it wants to.
Protect the people who **work the land**, not just the owners.
think: The **2029 renewal** likely comes before AGI, so the danger moves to the next lease.
She may be **ready to let go** by her mid-sixties anyway.
do: Agree a **stop date** with Tom, maybe 2033, while they still choose.
Sell the **oldest ten cows** and don't replace them, to save.
Push the estate, through the association, to pass the tenancy to a **young couple**.
feel: **Sad** but steadier: an ending she could plan, not one done to her.
S3.quote: An ending you can plan is sad, but an ending that's done to you is a different thing altogether.
fieldNote: Five years moves the threat past her **2029 renewal**, which changes everything for her.
Her **knees** may decide her exit before any robot does.
Still turns to the **association**, now to protect the next tenant rather than herself.

steps.text: Agree a stop date around 2033 with Tom
Sell the oldest ten cows and bank the money
Push the estate, through the association, to let a young couple take over

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning and nobody should waste it. People like me will be retired, so it's the young ones who need the rules sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, it barely touches me. Robots in 2039 means I'd be sixty-eight, and Tom and I mean to be out by then anyway. The 2029 lease and the one after it would both run as normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as we are, cows and barley, and plan to hand back the tenancy around 2034. I'd use the association to argue that the estate keeps letting farms to families. Otherwise nothing changes this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly settled. A bit worried for Danny and Ruth, but not for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about your son Danny and daughter Ruth?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My son Danny's an electrician, so he'll probably end up fixing the robots that replace his mother. It makes me laugh. Ruth's a nurse, and I can't see a robot holding a hand at a bedside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd change on the farm with that much warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe fix the calf shed roof properly, so whoever comes next gets a good farm. That's the kind of thing I care about at my age.

say: Ten years is **fair warning**, and nobody should waste it.
The young ones need the **rules sorted**, because people like her will be retired.
think: Robots in **2039** come when she's sixty-eight and already out.
Both the 2029 lease and the **next one** would run as normal.
do: Keep the **cows and barley** going as they are.
Plan to **hand back** the tenancy around 2034.
Use the association to keep the estate letting farms to **families**.
feel: Fairly **settled** for herself, a little **worried** for her grown-up children.
S4.quote: My son Danny's an electrician, so he'll probably end up fixing the robots that replace his mother.
fieldNote: With a decade's warning, her own **income and home** look safe until retirement.
Her care shifts to the **next tenant** and to leaving the farm in good shape.
Still keeps a background worry about the **2029 rent rise**, so not fully calm.

steps.text: Keep the cows and barley going as now
Plan to hand back the Hollins Farm tenancy around 2034
Fix the calf shed roof properly for the next tenant

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because it lands right on our lease. What would help is a law that a sitting tenant gets first refusal on renewal, and a fair payout if a landlord ends it early. Money to retrain at sixty would be no use to me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land, and that's the whole story. A tenant and an owner face the same robot very differently, and I don't think the people making the rules understand that.

headlineQuote: A tenant and an owner face the same robot very differently, and I don't think the people making the rules understand that.
portrait: Bianca, **58**, rents a 120-hectare beef and barley farm from an **estate** with her partner Tom.
She keeps the herd book on **paper** and leaves all screen work to Tom or a neighbour.
Her steady worry is the **2029 tenancy renewal**, which colours every scenario.
She turns to the **tenant association**, the MP and new laws rather than to technology.
Fast AGI frightens her most; a **ten-year** warning lets her plan a dignified exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the estate could end the lease in 2029 and plan robots for 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A law giving sitting tenants **first refusal** on renewal.
A **fair payout** if a landlord ends a tenancy early.
